subject: Religious and Moral Education
source: RELIGIOUS AND MORAL EDUCATION CURRICULUM FOR PRIMARY SCHOOLS (BASIC I - 6), September 2019
teacher_guidance: Read aloud when needed. Accept oral or written answers. Assess understanding of curriculum examples. For environmental topics, use age-appropriate examples and prioritise safety; no learner should handle polluted water or hazardous waste.

indicators.content_standard: B2.1.2.1. Appreciate the environment as God's creation
indicators.objective: Explain the importance of the environment.

skills.description: Recognise the examples and vocabulary in the lesson.
Explain meanings and connections in an example.

misconceptions: Thinking all surroundings are natural rather than partly human-made
Believing living things can survive without air, food, water, or shelter
Confusing human-made objects with natural creations
spec.difficultyPlan: 5 foundational, 7 simple-use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.

questions.stem: Which is a natural thing in the environment named in the curriculum?
hints: Choose something that grows naturally.
questions.explanation: Trees are examples of natural things in the curriculum.

questions.stem: Which object is made by people?
hints: People make furniture to sit on.
questions.explanation: A chair is human-made; stones, animals, and trees are examples of natural things.

questions.stem: Name one natural thing you might observe on a nature walk around school.
hints: Think of something not manufactured by people.
questions.explanation: The curriculum gives trees, stones, and animals as examples of natural things.

questions.stem: Which pair contains two human-made objects?
hints: Choose objects people construct or manufacture.
questions.explanation: Cars and tables are made by people. The other options list natural things.

questions.stem: Name one natural thing and one human-made thing you can see near your classroom.
hints: For example, a tree and a desk.
questions.explanation: Classify one observed natural feature and one object made by people.

criteria.description: Names a natural thing.
Names a human-made object.

questions.stem: Which is important for people and animals to breathe?
hints: Living things breathe it.
questions.explanation: Air is necessary for breathing and is one of the environmental needs named in the curriculum.

questions.stem: Which environmental need do people drink?
hints: It can be poured into a cup.
questions.explanation: Water is needed by people and other living things.

questions.stem: Name one thing people need from the environment to eat.
hints: The curriculum names this as a basic need.
questions.explanation: Food is one of the environmental needs listed in the curriculum.

questions.stem: Why is shelter important to people?
options: It helps protect people from weather and danger
It replaces the need to breathe
It makes people stop drinking water
It is food for every animal
hints: Think of a safe place to live.
questions.explanation: Shelter provides a place of protection and is one of the needs listed in the curriculum.

questions.stem: Name two environmental needs that help living things survive.
hints: Choose from air, food, water, and shelter.
questions.explanation: Any two of the four examples in the curriculum are acceptable.

criteria.description: Names two needs from air, food, water, and shelter.

questions.stem: Explain one way a tree or animal depends on its environment.
hints: Think about water, air, food, or a place to live.
questions.explanation: Living things rely on environmental conditions and resources for survival.

criteria.description: Names a relevant environmental need or condition.
Explains how it supports the chosen living thing.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the environment is important?
options: Living things depend on it for needs such as air, food, water, and shelter
It is only useful for making cars
People and animals do not need it
hints: Connect the environment to survival.
questions.explanation: The curriculum says the survival of God's creation depends on the environment.

questions.stem: A school garden has healthy soil, water, and air. Explain why these help plants live.
hints: Think about the needs of growing plants.
questions.explanation: Plants need suitable environmental conditions, including water and air, to grow.

criteria.description: Identifies at least one relevant need or condition.
Explains how it supports plant growth or survival.

questions.stem: What could happen to animals if their environment no longer provides food, water, or shelter?
hints: Think about how they would meet their basic needs.
questions.explanation: Animals may struggle to survive if essential needs are unavailable.

criteria.description: States that animals may become weak, move away, or fail to survive.
Links the outcome to missing needs.

questions.stem: A class wants to care for the school environment. Which action best supports living things?
options: Keep the area clean and protect plants
hints: Choose an action that protects shared surroundings.
questions.explanation: Keeping the area clean and protecting plants helps maintain a healthy environment.

questions.stem: Describe one way your class can keep its environment clean and explain who benefits.
hints: You could put litter in a bin or care for the garden.
questions.explanation: Practical care supports the wellbeing of learners and other living things.

criteria.description: Suggests a practical, safe action.
Identifies people, plants, animals, or the community as beneficiaries.

questions.stem: Explain how clean water in a community can help people, animals, and plants.
hints: Think of drinking, growing, and staying healthy.
questions.explanation: Clean water supports drinking, health, and plant growth for living things.

criteria.description: Gives a relevant benefit of clean water.
Connects the benefit to more than one living group or a clear survival need.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'The environment is only trees and animals.' Explain why the curriculum includes more than natural things.
hints: Remember that people also create buildings, cars, tables, and chairs.
questions.explanation: The environment includes natural things as well as human-made things and the surroundings in which life takes place.

criteria.description: Explains that human-made objects are also part of the surroundings.
Gives an accurate example of a human-made object.
Connects environment to the needs of living things.

questions.stem: Draw a healthy environment that provides at least two needs for living things. Label the needs and explain your drawing.
hints: Show, for example, clean water and plants or shelter.
questions.explanation: The drawing should represent environmental needs and how they support life. Artistic quality is not graded.

criteria.description: Shows a healthy environment.
Identifies two relevant needs.
Explains how the needs support living things.

questions.stem: Use one natural feature and one human-made object from a nature walk to explain how people depend on and shape their environment.
hints: For example, a tree and a classroom building.
questions.explanation: People depend on natural resources and also create objects and structures in their surroundings.

criteria.description: Names an accurate natural feature.
Names an accurate human-made object.
Explains dependence on or shaping of the environment.

indicators.content_standard: B2.1.2.1. Appreciate the environment as God's creation
indicators.objective: Demonstrate human activities that destroy God's creation or the environment.
curriculum_examples: Climate change heat, floods, rainstorms, less rainfall, drought, famine

skills.description: Recognise the examples and vocabulary in the lesson.
Explain meanings and connections in an example.
Apply the lesson to a situation and justify a choice.

misconceptions: Believing cutting every tree has no consequence
Confusing a natural hazard with a human activity that can worsen environmental harm
spec.difficultyPlan: 5 foundational, 7 simple-use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.

questions.stem: Which activity does the curriculum identify as harmful to the environment?
hints: Look for cutting trees without care or control.
questions.explanation: The curriculum identifies indiscriminate tree cutting as an activity that destroys the environment.

questions.stem: What name is commonly given to illegal mining activities in Ghana?
hints: The curriculum gives this Ghanaian term in brackets.
questions.explanation: The curriculum names illegal mining activities as galamsey.

questions.stem: Which action can pollute a water body?
options: Dumping rubbish or harmful waste into it
hints: Choose the action that makes the water dirty.
questions.explanation: Putting rubbish or harmful waste in water pollutes the water body.

questions.stem: Name one human activity from the curriculum that can damage the environment.
hints: Think of tree cutting, galamsey, or water pollution.
questions.explanation: Any one of the curriculum examples is acceptable.

criteria.description: Names one curriculum example accurately.

questions.stem: Which pair contains two harmful activities named in the curriculum?
hints: Look for activities the lesson says destroy or pollute.
questions.explanation: Illegal mining (galamsey) and pollution of water bodies are both listed as harmful.

questions.stem: Which problem can follow environmental destruction, according to the curriculum?
hints: Think of a long time with too little rain.
questions.explanation: Drought is one of the effects the curriculum lists.

questions.stem: Which event is listed as a possible effect of environmental destruction?
hints: It happens when water covers land that is usually dry.
questions.explanation: Floods are among the effects named in the curriculum.

questions.stem: Name one effect of environmental destruction from the curriculum besides floods.
hints: Choose from the list of weather and food problems.
questions.explanation: The curriculum lists heat, rainstorms, less rainfall, drought, and famine among possible effects.

questions.stem: Explain one way polluted water can harm living things that depend on it.
hints: Think about drinking water or living in the water.
questions.explanation: Polluted water can be unsafe for people and animals and can harm aquatic life.

criteria.description: Describes a plausible harm to people, animals, or aquatic life.
Connects the harm to polluted water.

questions.stem: How could cutting many trees affect people and animals who need the environment?
hints: Think about shade, shelter, and places where animals live.
questions.explanation: Removing trees can reduce shelter and affect habitats and environmental balance.

criteria.description: Names a relevant effect such as loss of shelter or habitat.
Explains who or what is affected.

questions.stem: A long period with less rainfall can make it harder to grow food. Which listed effect may follow?
hints: Think about dry conditions and not enough food.
questions.explanation: Less rainfall can contribute to drought, which may reduce food production and lead to famine.

questions.stem: The curriculum names heat, floods, rainstorms, less rainfall, drought, and famine. Give two examples of effects it asks learners to discuss.
hints: Choose any two from the list.
questions.explanation: Any two listed environmental effects are acceptable.

criteria.description: Names one listed effect accurately.
Names a second distinct listed effect accurately.

questions.stem: Describe one safe action a learner can take to help keep a nearby stream clean.
hints: Keep rubbish out of the water and tell a trusted adult about pollution.
questions.explanation: Children can avoid littering, use bins, and alert responsible adults. They should not handle hazardous waste or polluted water.

criteria.description: Suggests a safe, practical protective action.
Avoids unsafe contact with polluted water or waste.

questions.stem: A learner sees waste being dumped in a stream. What is the safest helpful response?
options: Stay away from the waste and tell a trusted adult
Touch the waste to identify it
Jump into the stream to remove it
hints: Choose the safe action for a child.
questions.explanation: A child should avoid hazardous waste and alert a trusted adult who can respond safely.

questions.stem: Suggest one way a community can reduce unnecessary cutting of trees.
hints: Think about protecting trees or planting replacements.
questions.explanation: Communities can protect existing trees, plant trees, and use resources responsibly.

criteria.description: Suggests a practical tree-protection or replanting action.
Explains how it helps the environment.

questions.stem: Draw a safe environment and an unsafe environment. Label one feature in each picture.
hints: A clean area with protected trees can contrast with polluted water or a damaged area.
questions.explanation: Represent a safe and unsafe environment using clear examples. Artistic quality is not graded.

criteria.description: Shows and labels one safe environmental feature.
Shows and labels one unsafe or damaged feature.

questions.stem: Explain why people should not pour harmful waste into rivers and streams.
hints: Think about drinking water and living things in the water.
questions.explanation: Pollution can make water unsafe and harm living things that depend on it.

criteria.description: Names a risk to people or animals.
Connects the risk to water pollution.

questions.stem: Your group is recording environmental problems for a class discussion. Name two harmful activities and one safe way to share your observations.
hints: Use the curriculum examples and tell an adult or report to the class.
questions.explanation: Learners may record observations about tree cutting, illegal mining, or water pollution and present them safely without approaching danger.

criteria.description: Names two curriculum-listed harmful activities.
Suggests a safe method of recording or presenting observations.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'Galamsey only changes the ground; it cannot affect the environment.' Explain why this claim needs care, using the curriculum's concerns about environmental damage.
hints: Illegal mining is listed as harmful; discuss possible effects without claiming every result is automatic.
questions.explanation: The curriculum identifies illegal mining as an activity that destroys the environment and lists broader environmental effects. Avoid asserting that any single activity automatically causes every listed effect.

criteria.description: Identifies galamsey as a harmful activity named in the curriculum.
Explains that environmental damage can affect land, water, or living things.
Avoids unsupported certainty about a particular effect.

questions.stem: Plan a short class message asking people to protect God's creation from tree destruction and water pollution. Include two actions people can take.
hints: Keep the message respectful and suggest safe actions.
questions.explanation: Create an age-appropriate message with two practical actions to care for trees and water.

criteria.description: Identifies tree destruction and water pollution as concerns.
Gives two practical protective actions.
Communicates respectfully and clearly.

uncertain: The curriculum lists climate change heat, floods, rainstorms, less rainfall, drought, and famine as effects of environmental destruction; questions preserve this list but avoid asserting that every listed effect follows automatically from each activity.

indicators.content_standard: B2.1.3.1. Appreciate things created by God
indicators.objective: Explain the purpose of God's creation.
curriculum_examples: Discuss the usefulness of plants and animals to humankind
Identify uses of animals and plants
Draw and colour useful plants and animals

skills.description: Recognise the examples and vocabulary in the lesson.
Explain meanings and connections in an example.
Apply the lesson to a situation and justify a choice.
Communicate understanding through a performance, drawing or demonstration.

misconceptions: Thinking plants and animals have no use to people
Believing every animal is safe to handle
Confusing usefulness with permission to harm or waste living things
spec.difficultyPlan: 5 foundational, 7 simple-use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.

questions.stem: Which plant is commonly used as food?
hints: It is a crop that people cook and eat.
questions.explanation: Maize is a plant crop used as food.

questions.stem: Name one plant people use for food.
hints: Think of a crop eaten in Ghana.
questions.explanation: Many plants provide food. Any suitable example is acceptable.

questions.stem: Which animal gives people eggs?
hints: It is a bird kept on some farms.
questions.explanation: Hens can provide eggs, an example of an animal's usefulness to people.

questions.stem: Name one useful thing people can get from a cow.
hints: Think of food or another product from a farm animal.
questions.explanation: Cows can provide milk, meat, leather, or manure, when cared for and used responsibly.

questions.stem: Name one useful plant and one useful animal, then say one use for each.
hints: For example, cassava for food and a hen for eggs.
questions.explanation: Give one plant and one animal and connect each with a sensible use.

criteria.description: Names a useful plant and gives a relevant use.
Names a useful animal and gives a relevant use.

questions.stem: How can trees be useful to people?
options: They can provide fruit, shade, or materials
They make people stop needing air
They are only useful when cut down carelessly
hints: Think about fruit trees and shade on a hot day.
questions.explanation: Trees can provide fruit, shade, and useful materials. They should be cared for responsibly.

questions.stem: Explain how a plant such as maize or cassava is useful to a family.
hints: Think about meals made from crops.
questions.explanation: Crops provide food and contribute to family nutrition.

criteria.description: Identifies the plant as a food crop or names a food made from it.
Explains its usefulness to the family.

questions.stem: A farmer keeps bees. Which useful product can bees help provide?
hints: It is a sweet food made by bees.
questions.explanation: Bees produce honey, a useful product. Bees also help pollinate many plants.

questions.stem: Describe one way animals can help people with food or farm work.
hints: Think about eggs, milk, meat, or an animal helping on a farm.
questions.explanation: Animals can provide food or assist with work, depending on the animal and local practice.

criteria.description: Names a plausible animal use.
Explains how it helps people.

questions.stem: What do some plants provide that people need to breathe?
hints: Plants help keep the air suitable for life.
questions.explanation: Plants contribute oxygen to the air, which people and animals need for breathing.

questions.stem: How can plants and animals together help provide food for people? Give one example of each.
hints: A crop and a farm animal can both provide food.
questions.explanation: Plants such as maize provide crop foods; animals such as hens provide eggs or meat.

criteria.description: Gives a plant food example.
Gives an animal food example.
Explains that both contribute to people's food.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes why the curriculum asks learners to study useful plants and animals?
options: To understand how creation supports human life
To learn that plants and animals should be wasted
To prove that people do not need nature
To encourage children to harm animals
hints: The indicator asks about usefulness to humankind.
questions.explanation: The curriculum directs learners to discuss the usefulness of plants and animals to people.

questions.stem: Choose one useful plant and explain how you could show its usefulness in a drawing.
hints: You might draw a food crop beside a meal made from it.
questions.explanation: Connect the plant representation to a use such as food, shade, or material.

criteria.description: Names a plant and a relevant use.
Describes a drawing that makes the use clear.

questions.stem: Draw one useful animal and show or label one way it helps people.
hints: A hen with eggs or a cow with milk are examples.
questions.explanation: Represent an animal and its usefulness. Artistic skill is not assessed.

criteria.description: Draws or clearly identifies a useful animal.
Shows or labels a valid use.

questions.stem: A classmate says trees are useful only after they are cut down. Give two other useful roles of living trees.
hints: Think about fruit, shade, habitats, or helping the environment.
questions.explanation: Living trees can provide shade, fruit, habitats, and environmental benefits without being cut down.

criteria.description: Names one useful role of a living tree.
Names a second distinct role.

questions.stem: Why should people care for useful animals instead of being cruel to them?
hints: They are living things and can support people's needs.
questions.explanation: Animals are living things that may provide food or other benefits; responsible care avoids unnecessary suffering.

criteria.description: Recognises animals as living things deserving care.
Mentions a valid usefulness to people.

questions.stem: Make a two-part picture: one useful plant and one useful animal. Label one benefit from each.
hints: Show a plant food and an animal product or service.
questions.explanation: Show and label a useful plant and a useful animal and connect each to a benefit.

criteria.description: Shows and labels a plant with a valid benefit.
Shows and labels an animal with a valid benefit.

questions.stem: Explain how a plant and an animal can each help meet people's needs, and give one example of caring for each responsibly.
hints: Match each example to a need and a safe care action.
questions.explanation: Connect one plant and one animal to human usefulness while describing responsible stewardship.

criteria.description: Explains a useful role of a plant.
Explains a useful role of an animal.
Gives a responsible care action for both or clearly for each.

questions.stem: Your group is making a class display about useful creation. Choose a plant and an animal and explain why neither should be wasted or treated carelessly.
hints: Consider their usefulness and their value as living things.
questions.explanation: Explain both usefulness and care for living things, in line with the curriculum's appreciation and caring practices.

criteria.description: Gives one valid plant example and its use.
Gives one valid animal example and its use.
Explains responsible care or avoiding waste.

questions.stem: Give a short presentation explaining the purpose of God's creation using one useful plant and one useful animal as examples.
hints: Name each example, say how it is useful, and connect your answer to the curriculum.
questions.explanation: Use the indicator's focus: discuss usefulness of plants and animals to humankind, with respectful appreciation.

criteria.description: Names a useful plant and explains its contribution.
Names a useful animal and explains its contribution.
Connects the examples to appreciation of creation.

uncertain: The curriculum asks learners to explain the purpose of God's creation and specifically directs discussion of plants' and animals' usefulness to humankind; questions follow those stated exemplars without extending them into unsupported claims about a single exclusive purpose.
